24.explanation:
Correct answer: B — Syndesmosis

Why this is correct:
- The inferior (distal) tibiofibular joint is a fibrous joint in which the fibular notch of the distal tibia and the medial surface of the fibula are united by a strong interosseous ligament, reinforced by the anterior and posterior inferior tibiofibular ligaments and the transverse ligament.
- Because the two bones are joined by ligamentous tissue rather than by hyaline cartilage, fibrocartilage, or a synovial cavity, the joint is classified as a syndesmosis — a fibrous joint permitting only minimal movement (slight separation during dorsiflexion).
- Its mechanical role is to hold the fibula firmly against the tibia so that the talus remains within the ankle mortise; the superior (proximal) tibiofibular joint, in contrast, is a small synovial joint.
- Clinically, forced external rotation of the ankle can tear this syndesmosis (a 'high ankle sprain'); widening of the tibiofibular clear space on radiographs may require screw fixation.

Clinical reasoning:
| Step | Finding | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Articulation between the distal ends of tibia and fibula at the ankle mortise | Must resist diastasis while allowing a few millimetres of movement in dorsiflexion |
| 2 | Bones united by the interosseous and inferior tibiofibular ligaments | Ligamentous union defines a fibrous joint, specifically a syndesmosis |
| 3 | No cartilage plate, fibrocartilaginous disc, or synovial cavity is interposed | Excludes synchondrosis, symphysis and synovial joint classifications |

Why other options are wrong:
- Option A — Synchondrosis is a primary cartilaginous joint united by hyaline cartilage (for example, an epiphysial plate or the first sternocostal joint), not a ligamentous union.
- Option C — Symphysis is a secondary cartilaginous joint in which fibrocartilage separates the bones, as in the pubic symphysis and intervertebral discs; this is not the ankle joint.
- Option D — Schindylesis is an uncommon fibrous joint in which a thin bony ridge fits into a groove, as between the vomer and the palate/maxilla; it is not found at the ankle.

Key points:
- Inferior (distal) tibiofibular joint = syndesmosis (fibrous); superior (proximal) tibiofibular joint = synovial.
- Common exam trap: do not confuse the tibiofibular syndesmosis with the talocrural (ankle) joint, which is a synovial hinge joint.

Reference: Last's Anatomy, 13th edition, section on joints of the lower limb; OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 9.2 Fibrous joints (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/9-2-fibrous-joints); StatPearls, Distal Tibiofibular Joint (https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK547655/)
24.source: Last's Anatomy 13/e (ankle joints); OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e 9.2; StatPearls NBK547655 (checked via web search)

103.explanation:
Correct answers: A, B, D, E — Tunica media of ascending aorta; Connective tissue of thymus gland; Choroid & sclera of eye; Mandible bone

Why this is correct:
- Neural crest cells are an ectoderm-derived, migratory population that forms ectomesenchyme in the head and neck: connective tissue, smooth muscle, cartilage and bone. Cardiac neural crest additionally builds the wall of the large arteries arising from the heart.
- Option A: cardiac neural crest contributes the musculoconnective tissue wall (tunica media) of the ascending aorta and proximal great vessels. Gilbert's table lists 'connective tissue and smooth muscle in arteries of aortic arch origin' as a neural crest derivative; the tunica media of the descending aorta is mesodermal, so the proximal location matters.
- Option B: thymic epithelium comes from the third pharyngeal pouch endoderm, but the connective tissue stroma/capsule of the thymus is neural-crest mesenchyme.
- Option D: periocular neural crest forms the choroid and sclera (as well as corneal stroma/endothelium); the retina itself is neural ectoderm, but its two outer coats named here are crest-derived.
- Option E: the mandible is a first pharyngeal arch bone formed from cranial neural crest mesenchyme of the mandibular prominence.
- Option C is excluded: enamel is secreted by ameloblasts of surface (oral) ectoderm. Dentine and pulp, by contrast, come from neural-crest odontoblasts and mesenchyme — a classic examination trap.

Clinical reasoning:
| Step | Finding | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Question asks for neural crest derivatives | Must distinguish crest/ectomesenchyme from surface ectoderm, endoderm and mesoderm |
| 2 | Ascending aortic media, thymic connective tissue, choroid and sclera, mandible | All are neural-crest connective tissue, smooth muscle or skeletal derivatives |
| 3 | Enamel of teeth | Surface ectoderm (ameloblasts), therefore not a correct letter |

Why other options are wrong:
- Option C — Enamel is not a neural crest derivative; it is laid down by ameloblasts derived from surface ectoderm. Only dentine (odontoblasts) and dental pulp are neural crest related.

Key points:
- Head and neck connective tissue and bone = neural crest; tooth enamel = surface ectoderm; thymic epithelium = endoderm, thymic connective tissue = neural crest.
- Exam trap: cardiac crest supplies the ascending aorta and arch; the descending aortic media is mesodermal.

Reference: Gilbert SF, Developmental Biology, 6th edition, Table 13.1 'Some derivatives of the neural crest' (NCBI Bookshelf: https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK10065/table/A3110/); UNSW Embryology, Neural Crest Development (https://embryology.med.unsw.edu.au/embryology/index.php/Neural_Crest_Development); Last's Anatomy 13/e, embryology section.
103.source: Gilbert Developmental Biology 6/e Table 13.1 (NCBI Bookshelf, checked); UNSW Embryology Neural Crest Development (checked); Last's Anatomy 13/e

109.explanation:
Correct answer: D — Adrenal cortex

Why this is correct:
- The ectoderm gives surface ectoderm (epidermis and its glands, enamel, anterior pituitary) and neural ectoderm (neural tube, brain and spinal cord, retina, posterior pituitary, neural crest derivatives). The question asks for the single exception, i.e. the structure that is not ectodermal.
- Hypophysis (pituitary gland) has a dual ectodermal origin: the adenohypophysis arises from Rathke's pouch of the oral surface ectoderm, and the neurohypophysis from the infundibulum of the diencephalic neural ectoderm.
- The retina develops from the optic cup, an outgrowth of the forebrain neural ectoderm; the spinal cord develops from the neural tube, also neural ectoderm.
- The adrenal cortex arises from intermediate mesoderm (coelomic epithelium of the urogenital ridge). Only the adrenal medulla is derived from neural crest cells — a frequent point of confusion.
- Therefore adrenal cortex is the only mesodermal option and is the correct 'except' answer.

Clinical reasoning:
| Step | Finding | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Stem asks 'all are derived from ectoderm except' | Identify the one mesodermal structure among four candidates |
| 2 | Hypophysis, retina and spinal cord | Each is surface or neural ectoderm in origin |
| 3 | Adrenal cortex | Intermediate mesoderm; the medulla is the ectodermal/neural crest part |

Why other options are wrong:
- Option A — Hypophysis is ectodermal: anterior lobe from oral ectoderm (Rathke's pouch), posterior lobe from neural ectoderm.
- Option B — Retina is neural ectoderm, being the sensory layer of the optic cup derived from the forebrain.
- Option C — Spinal cord is derived from the neural tube, a neural ectodermal structure.

Key points:
- Adrenal gland is a germ-layer hybrid: cortex = mesoderm, medulla = neural crest (ectoderm).
- Exam trap: the pituitary's two lobes have different ectodermal sources, but both are ectoderm, so neither is the exception.

Reference: Langman's Medical Embryology, germ-layer derivatives and endocrine gland development; UNSW Embryology, Endocrine System Development (https://embryology.med.unsw.edu.au/embryology/index.php/Endocrine_System_Development); Gilbert SF, Developmental Biology 6/e, neural crest chapter (https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK10065/).
109.source: Langman's Medical Embryology (germ layer derivatives); UNSW Embryology Endocrine System Development (checked); Gilbert Developmental Biology 6/e (checked)

135.explanation:
Correct answer: C — Two arteries and the left vein

Why this is correct:
- The mature umbilical cord normally contains three vessels: two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein. The vessels lie within Wharton's jelly, surrounded by amnion.
- Early in gestation there are paired umbilical arteries and paired umbilical veins. The right umbilical vein regresses (by about the 6th to 8th week), so the left umbilical vein is the single vein that persists and carries oxygenated, nutrient-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus.
- Both umbilical arteries persist; they arise from the fetal internal iliac (hypogastric) arteries and carry deoxygenated blood back to the placenta. After birth their intra-abdominal remnants become the medial umbilical ligaments, while the left umbilical vein becomes the round ligament of the liver.
- Therefore the correct description of the vessels is two arteries and the left vein.

Clinical reasoning:
| Step | Finding | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Question on the vessels normally present in the cord | Expect three vessels: two arteries and one vein |
| 2 | Which vein remains | The right umbilical vein involutes; the left persists and joins the ductus venosus |
| 3 | Clinical correlation | A two-vessel cord (single umbilical artery) is a common anomaly associated with congenital abnormalities |

Why other options are wrong:
- Option A — Two arteries and two veins describes the transient early embryonic arrangement; persistence of both veins gives a rare four-vessel cord, not the normal cord.
- Option B — One artery and one vein is a two-vessel cord (single umbilical artery), an anomaly rather than the normal pattern.
- Option D — Two veins and the left artery is wrong on both counts: both arteries normally persist and it is the right vein, not an artery, that disappears.

Key points:
- Normal cord: two arteries (deoxygenated to placenta) and one left vein (oxygenated to fetus).
- Exam trap: arteries and veins are named by direction relative to the fetal heart, not by oxygen content.

Reference: Last's Anatomy, 13th edition, embryology and placenta; StatPearls, Anatomy, Abdomen and Pelvis: Umbilical Cord (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557389/); StatPearls, Embryology, Umbilical Cord (https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557490/).
135.source: Last's Anatomy 13/e; StatPearls Umbilical Cord NBK557389 and NBK557490 (checked via web search)

136.explanation:
Correct answer: C — Right umbilical vein disappears

Why this is correct:
- Paired umbilical veins are present early in embryonic life, draining into the sinus venosus. During the second month the right umbilical vein undergoes atresia and disappears, leaving the left umbilical vein as the sole venous channel in the cord.
- The left umbilical vein continues to enlarge, enters the left portal vein and is joined by the ductus venosus, which shunts much of the placental blood directly to the inferior vena cava.
- Both umbilical arteries persist, so the normal cord has three vessels: two arteries and one vein. This makes options A and B incorrect.
- The normal cord at term measures roughly 50 to 60 cm in length, so the 25-30 cm stated in option D is too short; cords under about 30-35 cm are classified as short cords.
- Thus the only true statement among the choices is that the right umbilical vein disappears.

Clinical reasoning:
| Step | Finding | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 'True about umbilical cord' | Test number of vessels, regression of veins and normal length |
| 2 | Right umbilical vein regresses by 6-8 weeks | The left vein remains the single cord vein |
| 3 | Persistence of a right vein or loss of an artery | Four-vessel cord or single umbilical artery, both clinically significant anomalies |

Why other options are wrong:
- Option A — Contains two umbilical veins: not normal; a four-vessel cord with persistent right vein is an uncommon anomaly associated with cardiovascular and gastrointestinal defects.
- Option B — Contains one umbilical artery: the normal cord has two arteries; a single umbilical artery is an anomaly.
- Option D — Length is 25-30 cm: that is a short cord; a normal term cord averages 50-60 cm (up to 70 cm in some texts).

Key points:
- Right umbilical vein disappears; left umbilical vein persists and later becomes the round ligament of the liver.
- Exam trap: remember the cord length is about 50-60 cm at term, not 25-30 cm.

Reference: Last's Anatomy 13/e, placenta and cord; StatPearls, Anatomy, Abdomen and Pelvis: Umbilical Cord (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557389/); UNSW Embryology, Placenta - Cord (https://embryology.med.unsw.edu.au/embryology/index.php/Placenta_-_Cord).
136.source: Last's Anatomy 13/e; StatPearls NBK557389; UNSW Embryology Placenta-Cord (all checked)

979.explanation:
Correct answer: A — Vertebral arteries (printed key; see caveat below)

Why this is correct:
- In postductal (adult) coarctation the narrowing lies just distal to the ductus arteriosus/ligamentum arteriosum, so blood must reach the descending aorta and lower body through collateral channels connecting subclavian and axillary branches above the obstruction with intercostal, epigastric and iliac vessels below it.
- The standard textbook collateral routes are: internal thoracic artery to superior epigastric to inferior epigastric and external iliac; the axillary artery via subscapular, lateral thoracic and thoracoacromial branches and the suprascapular/descending scapular network into posterior intercostal arteries; and posterior intercostals from the descending aorta itself, with additional direct mediastinal branches.
- The vertebral artery is principally a cerebral vessel that joins the basilar artery at the pontine border. It is not among the named vessels in Gray's Anatomy's account of the collateral circulation of postductal coarctation, which is why the printed key selects it.
- Original source explanation preserved verbatim: This is a controversial question, with no answer, as all of the given arteries participate in the anastomosis. Since Gray’s anatomy has no mention of vertebral artery in the topic, that has been taken as the answer of choice.
- Imaging literature does list vertebral and anterior spinal arteries among the less frequent collateral channels in coarctation, so the item is genuinely contentious: the key is an examination convention rather than proof that the vertebral artery can never participate.

Clinical reasoning:
| Step | Finding | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Postductal coarctation with distal anastomoses | Proximal (upper body) pressure is high; the lower body relies on collaterals |
| 2 | Dilated posterior intercostal and internal thoracic vessels on imaging | They bypass the stenosis and produce the characteristic rib notching |
| 3 | Candidate not in the standard textbook collateral list | The vertebral artery is selected by exclusion in the printed key |

Why other options are wrong:
- Option B — Axillary artery branches (subscapular, lateral thoracic, thoracoacromial) form the parascapular collateral network that feeds posterior intercostals distal to the coarctation; it is a recognised participant.
- Option C — Subscapular and suprascapular arteries form the scapular anastomosis connecting the upper and lower systems through the intercostals; these are classical collaterals.
- Option D — Posterior intercostal arteries are the central distal pathway of the bypass; their enlargement grooves the inferior rib margins and produces rib notching.

Key points:
- Classic coarctation collaterals: internal thoracic-epigastric, parascapular (subscapular/suprascapular), posterior intercostal and mediastinal channels.
- Exam trap: some keys exclude the vertebral artery because standard anatomy texts omit it from the list, even though radiological case series document it.

Reference: Gray's Anatomy, 41st edition, thoracic wall and coarctation collateral circulation; Last's Anatomy, 13th edition, thorax; Radiology: Cardiothoracic Imaging, Collateral Circulation in Coarctation (https://pubs.rsna.org/doi/10.1148/ryct.240250); AJR 1986, Mediastinal collateral arteries (https://ajronline.org/doi/pdf/10.2214/ajr.146.4.757).
979.source: Gray's Anatomy 41/e and Last's Anatomy 13/e (standard collateral lists); Radiology Cardiothoracic Imaging 2024 and AJR 1986 (checked); original source explanation preserved
979.notes: Controversial item flagged in the source: the original explanation states there is no true answer because all listed arteries can participate, and that vertebral artery is chosen only because Gray's does not mention it in this topic. Printed key (A) retained unchanged. Peer-reviewed imaging literature does document vertebral/anterior spinal collaterals.

981.explanation:
Correct answer: A — Vertebral artery (printed key; see caveat below)

Why this is correct:
- In postductal coarctation of the aorta, blood reaches the descending aorta below the stenosis through anastomoses between branches of the subclavian and axillary arteries above and intercostal, epigastric and iliac vessels below.
- The classical collateral pathways are the internal thoracic artery (from the subclavian) anastomosing with posterior intercostal arteries and, via the superior epigastric, with the inferior epigastric artery from the external iliac; the suprascapular and descending scapular arteries anastomosing with subscapular/circumflex scapular branches of the axillary and with posterior intercostals; and direct mediastinal collateral arteries.
- The vertebral artery ascends through the cervical transverse foramina to form the basilar artery for the brain. It is not part of the standard textbook list of distal anastomotic channels in this topic, so the printed key correctly identifies it as the exception.
- Original source explanation preserved verbatim: This question has no answer, as all of the given arteries participate in the anastomosis. Since Gray’s anatomy has no mention of vertebral artery in the topic, that becomes the answer of choice.
- Modern angiographic studies describe vertebral and anterior spinal arteries as occasional additional collaterals; accordingly this question is contentious and should be read as testing the textbook list rather than absolute anatomical impossibility.

Clinical reasoning:
| Step | Finding | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 'Collaterals are formed by all EXCEPT' | Find the vessel omitted from the standard collateral pathways |
| 2 | Internal thoracic, suprascapular and posterior intercostal arteries | All are directly involved in bypassing the coarctation |
| 3 | Vertebral artery | Primarily cerebral; excluded by the textbook convention used for the key |

Why other options are wrong:
- Option B — Suprascapular artery, a branch of the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian, anastomoses around the scapula with axillary branches and posterior intercostals; it is a genuine collateral.
- Option C — Posterior intercostal arteries receive the collateral流入 from the upper system and enter the descending aorta; they are always involved and cause rib notching when enlarged.
- Option D — Internal thoracic artery connects superiorly via the subclavian and inferiorly with the inferior epigastric artery, one of the most important bypass routes.

Key points:
- Memorise the coarctation bypass: subclavian/internal thoracic, scapular anastomosis, posterior intercostals, epigastrics, mediastinal branches.
- Exam trap: the vertebral artery is excluded in standard MCQ keys despite occasional radiological participation.

Reference: Gray's Anatomy, 41st edition, collateral circulation in coarctation; Last's Anatomy, 13th edition, thorax; Radiology: Cardiothoracic Imaging, Collateral Circulation in Coarctation (https://pubs.rsna.org/doi/10.1148/ryct.240250); AJR 1986 (https://ajronline.org/doi/pdf/10.2214/ajr.146.4.757).
981.source: Gray's Anatomy 41/e and Last's Anatomy 13/e (standard lists); Radiology Cardiothoracic Imaging 2024; AJR 1986; original source explanation preserved
981.notes: Same controversy as item 980: the source explanation says no option is truly excluded and the vertebral artery is chosen because Gray's omits it from this topic. Printed key (A) unchanged. Peer-reviewed sources list vertebral/anterior spinal arteries as infrequent collaterals.

1190.explanation:
Correct answer: D — Extensor carpi ulnaris

Why this is correct:
- The anatomical snuff box is a triangular depression on the dorsolateral aspect of the wrist and hand, best seen when the thumb is fully extended and abducted.
- Its radial (lateral) border is formed by the tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis; its ulnar (medial) border is the tendon of extensor pollicis longus. Proximally it is bounded by the radial styloid process and distally by the base of the first metacarpal.
- The floor is formed by the scaphoid and trapezium, and the contents include the radial artery, the cephalic vein and the superficial branch of the radial nerve.
- Extensor carpi ulnaris runs along the ulnar side of the forearm and inserts on the base of the fifth metacarpal; it does not form any boundary of the snuff box. Therefore it is the correct 'EXCEPT' answer.

Clinical reasoning:
| Step | Finding | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Depression visible on the radial side with the thumb extended | Boundaries are the three thumb tendons: APL, EPB and EPL |
| 2 | Radial artery traverses the floor | A convenient pulse point and a guide to the scaphoid |
| 3 | Tenderness over the floor after a fall on the outstretched hand | Suspect scaphoid fracture; immobilise and image even if initial X-ray is normal |

Why other options are wrong:
- Option A — Abductor pollicis longus tendon forms the lateral (radial) border together with EPB, so it is a genuine boundary and is not the exception.
- Option B — Extensor pollicis longus tendon forms the medial (ulnar) border of the snuff box, so it is not the exception.
- Option C — Extensor pollicis brevis tendon forms the lateral border with APL; it is a boundary, not an outlier.

Key points:
- Snuff box borders: APL + EPB laterally, EPL medially; floor = scaphoid and trapezium.
- Exam trap: ECU and extensor carpi radialis muscles move the wrist but do not bound the snuff box.

Reference: Last's Anatomy, 13th edition, upper limb surface anatomy; TeachMeAnatomy, The Anatomical Snuffbox - Borders and Contents (https://teachmeanatomy.info/upper-limb/areas/anatomical-snuffbox/); StatPearls, Anatomical Snuff Box (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK482228/).
1190.source: Last's Anatomy 13/e; TeachMeAnatomy snuffbox; StatPearls NBK482228 (checked via web search)

1226.explanation:
Correct answer: A — L1 (the fundus of the gallbladder lies at the transpyloric plane, lower border of L1)

Why this is correct:
- The transpyloric plane (Addison's plane) is an imaginary horizontal plane set approximately at the level of the first lumbar vertebra, midway between the xiphoid process and the umbilicus.
- Structures classically intersected by it include the pylorus, the first part of the duodenum, the neck of the pancreas, the origin of the superior mesenteric artery, the renal hila, the duodenojejunal flexure and the fundus of the gallbladder.
- The fundus of the gallbladder is projected on the anterior abdominal wall at the junction of the ninth costal cartilage and the lateral border of the rectus abdominis, which is conventionally described at the transpyloric plane, i.e. L1.
- Cadaveric studies show that the fundus often lies a little below the plane, but for standard anatomy examinations the transpyloric plane/L1 remains the accepted surface-marking answer.

Clinical reasoning:
| Step | Finding | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Asked for the vertebral level of the gallbladder fundus | Recall the surface marking at the ninth costal cartilage |
| 2 | Ninth costal cartilage corresponds to the transpyloric plane | Transpyloric plane is at L1 |
| 3 | Clinical application | Gallbladder tenderness is elicited below the right costal margin (Murphy's sign) in cholecystitis |

Why other options are wrong:
- Option B — L3 corresponds roughly to the subcostal plane, well below the gallbladder fundus; it is not the transpyloric level.
- Option C — S1 is the level of the sacral promontory/sacroiliac region, far too low for an upper abdominal organ.
- Option D — S3 is even lower in the pelvis and has no relation to gallbladder surface anatomy.

Key points:
- Transpyloric plane = L1; subcostal plane = L3; intercristal/supracristal plane = L4; transtubercular plane = L5.
- Exam trap: barium/CT studies show anatomical variation, but textbook surface anatomy uses L1.

Reference: Last's Anatomy, 13th edition, surface anatomy of the abdomen; Gray's Anatomy, 41st edition, transpyloric plane; Radiopaedia, Vertebral levels (anatomical landmarks) (https://radiopaedia.org/articles/vertebral-levels-anatomical-landmarks).
1226.source: Last's Anatomy 13/e; Gray's Anatomy 41/e; Radiopaedia vertebral levels (checked); standard surface-anatomy convention
1226.notes: Standard textbook/exam convention (transpyloric plane, L1). Cadaver studies report the gallbladder fundus below this plane in many subjects; printed key retained.

1227.explanation:
Correct answer: B — L4 (the highest point of the iliac crest lies at the level of the L4 vertebral spine)

Why this is correct:
- A line joining the highest points of the two iliac crests is the supracristal (intercristal) plane, also known as Tuffier's line. It is the standard surface landmark used to identify the L4 vertebra before lumbar puncture or epidural anaesthesia, typically at the L4/L5 interspace.
- In textbook surface anatomy this plane passes through the spine of L4; therefore the vertebral level asked for is L4.
- Other surface planes provide useful contrasts: the transpyloric plane at L1, the subcostal plane at L3, the transtubercular plane at L5, and the posterior superior iliac spines at about S2.
- Modern imaging studies show the intercristal line may cross L4 or L5 depending on sex and habitus, but the conventional examination answer remains L4.

Clinical reasoning:
| Step | Finding | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Highest point of the iliac crest palpated | Used to draw Tuffier's (intercristal) line |
| 2 | Plane crosses the L4 vertebra/L4-5 interspace | Identifies the level for lumbar puncture |
| 3 | Needle inserted in the midline below this landmark | Enters the subarachnoid space below the conus medullaris |

Why other options are wrong:
- Option A — L3 corresponds to the subcostal plane, which lies above the iliac crests; it is not the level of the highest point of the crest.
- Option C — L5 corresponds roughly to the transtubercular plane through the iliac tubercles, below the crestal tips.
- Option D — S1 relates to the sacral promontory and sacroiliac articulation, not to the iliac crest.

Key points:
- Iliac crest highest point = L4; use it to find the L4/L5 space for lumbar puncture.
- Exam trap: remembering the whole sequence of abdominal planes prevents level mix-ups.

Reference: Last's Anatomy, 13th edition, surface anatomy of the abdomen and back; Gray's Anatomy, 41st edition, vertebral levels; Radiopaedia, Vertebral levels and Intercristal line (https://radiopaedia.org/articles/intercristal-line-1?lang=us).
1227.source: Last's Anatomy 13/e; Gray's Anatomy 41/e; Radiopaedia intercristal line (checked); standard surface-anatomy convention
1227.notes: Textbook convention is L4; imaging studies show the intercristal line can cross L4 or L5 depending on sex and build. Printed key retained.

1234.explanation:
Correct answer: B — Genitofemoral nerve

Why this is correct:
- The rectus sheath is the fibrous envelope enclosing the rectus abdominis muscle. Its contents classically include rectus abdominis, the pyramidalis muscle in the lower part, the superior and inferior epigastric arteries and veins, lymphatics, and the terminal anterior rami of the lower intercostal (thoracoabdominal) and subcostal nerves, T7 to T12.
- The genitofemoral nerve arises from the lumbar plexus (L1, L2) and emerges from the medial border of psoas major. Its genital branch enters the inguinal canal with the spermatic cord or round ligament, and its femoral branch passes beneath the inguinal ligament into the femoral triangle.
- Neither branch enters the rectus sheath, so genitofemoral nerve is the exception.
- Related nerves such as the ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric lie close to the inguinal canal and lower abdominal wall but are also not contents of the sheath; the key distinction is that the sheath carries thoracoabdominal nerves and epigastric vessels.

Clinical reasoning:
| Step | Finding | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Question lists possible contents of the rectus sheath | Recall the sheath's normal contents: muscle, epigastric vessels, T7-T12 nerves |
| 2 | Genitofemoral nerve arises from L1-L2 lumbar plexus | Its course is retroperitoneal and inguinal, not within the sheath |
| 3 | Surgical relevance | Inguinal and retropubic approaches must preserve these nerves and the epigastric vessels |

Why other options are wrong:
- Option A — Pyramidalis muscle lies within the rectus sheath, anterior to the lower part of rectus abdominis, and is therefore a genuine content.
- Option C — Inferior epigastric vessels ascend from the external iliac artery and enter the sheath below the arcuate ligament, running posterior to rectus abdominis.
- Option D — Superior epigastric vessels descend from the internal thoracic artery into the sheath and anastomose with the inferior epigastric vessels.

Key points:
- Rectus sheath contents: rectus abdominis, pyramidalis, superior and inferior epigastric vessels, lower five intercostal and subcostal nerves.
- Exam trap: nerves of the lumbar plexus (ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric, genitofemoral) are not inside the sheath despite supplying the groin.

Reference: Last's Anatomy, 13th edition, anterior abdominal wall and rectus sheath; StatPearls, Anatomy, Abdomen and Pelvis, Rectus Sheath (https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537153/); Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Rectus Sheath (https://www.elsevier.com/resources/anatomy/muscular-system/muscles-of-abdomen/rectus-sheath/18648).
1234.source: Last's Anatomy 13/e; StatPearls NBK537153; Elsevier Complete Anatomy rectus sheath (checked via web search)

1240.explanation:
Correct answer: A — Subcostal nerve

Why this is correct:
- Pyramidalis is a small triangular muscle lying in the lowest part of the rectus sheath, anterior to the lower fibres of rectus abdominis. It arises from the pubic crest and pubic symphysis and inserts into the linea alba; its action is to tense the linea alba.
- Its motor supply is from the subcostal nerve, the ventral ramus of T12. Its blood supply is from the inferior epigastric artery.
- The muscle is inconstant, being absent in a significant minority of individuals, but when present its nerve supply is the subcostal nerve in standard anatomy texts.
- The other listed nerves are lumbar plexus branches that supply groin skin and other abdominal muscles or the genital/femoral regions, not pyramidalis.

Clinical reasoning:
| Step | Finding | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Small triangular muscle anterior to lower rectus | Identifies pyramidalis |
| 2 | Segmental level of the lower anterior abdominal wall | T12 subcostal nerve supplies it |

1241.explanation:
Correct answer: A — Xiphoid process

Why this is correct:
- Rectus abdominis is a paired vertical muscle of the anterior abdominal wall enclosed in the rectus sheath. It arises inferiorly from the pubic crest and pubic symphysis and ascends to insert superiorly into the xiphoid process and the anterior aspects of the costal cartilages of ribs 5 to 7.
- Because the question asks specifically for an insertion of the muscle, the xiphoid process is the correct option among those offered.
- The linea alba (median raphe) is not a muscular insertion: it is the midline fibrous raphe formed by the interlacing aponeuroses of the external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominis, with rectus abdominis lying on either side of it.
- Ribs 1 to 4 have no rectus abdominis attachment; pectoralis major and other chest wall muscles attach to upper costal cartilages instead.

Clinical reasoning:
| Step | Finding | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rectus abdominis runs vertically in the anterior abdominal wall | Origin is pubic crest/symphysis, insertion is superior |
| 2 | Superior attachment sought | Xiphoid process and costal cartilages 5-7 are the true insertions |
| 3 | Distinguish muscle insertion from aponeurotic raphe | Linea alba/median raphe is formed by the flat muscles' aponeuroses |

Why other options are wrong:
- Option B — Median raphe is another name for the linea alba; rectus muscle fibres do not insert into it, the aponeuroses of the flat abdominal muscles do.
- Option C — Linea alba is the midline tendinous intersection of the abdominal aponeuroses, not the insertion of rectus abdominis.
- Option D — Ribs 1-4 are too high and are not attachment sites; the muscle reaches only costal cartilages 5 to 7.

Key points:
- Rectus abdominis: pubic crest/symphysis to xiphoid process and costal cartilages 5-7; flexes the trunk and tenses the abdominal wall.
- Exam trap: linea alba and median raphe are aponeurotic structures, not muscle insertions.

1257.explanation:
Correct answer: C — Right gastroepiploic artery

Why this is correct:
- The splenic artery is the largest branch of the coeliac trunk. It runs a tortuous course along the superior border of the pancreas toward the splenic hilum and gives off posterior gastric arteries, short gastric arteries to the fundus, left gastroepiploic (left gastro-omental) artery, pancreatic branches including the arteria pancreatica magna, and terminal hilar branches that enter the spleen.
- The right gastroepiploic (right gastro-omental) artery arises instead from the gastroduodenal artery, which is a branch of the common hepatic artery, another division of the coeliac trunk. It runs along the greater curvature on the right and anastomoses with the left gastroepiploic artery.
- Therefore the right gastroepiploic artery is not a branch of the splenic artery and is the correct EXCEPT answer.
- Clinical relevance: the gastroepiploic arcade along the greater curvature is important in gastric surgery, and the right gastroepiploic artery is sometimes used as a coronary artery bypass conduit.

Clinical reasoning:
| Step | Finding | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Coeliac trunk divides into left gastric, common hepatic and splenic arteries | Establish which parent vessel gives each named branch |
| 2 | Short gastrics, hilar branches and pancreatica magna arise from the splenic artery | These are genuine splenic branches |
| 3 | Right gastroepiploic comes from gastroduodenal/common hepatic | It is the exception |

Why other options are wrong:
- Option A — Short gastric arteries arise from the distal splenic artery near the hilum and supply the fundus of the stomach; they are genuine splenic branches.
- Option B — Hilar (terminal) branches are the direct splenic artery branches entering the splenic hilum.
- Option D — Arteria pancreatica magna is a large pancreatic branch of the splenic artery supplying the body and tail of the pancreas.

Key points:
- Splenic artery branches: short gastric, left gastroepiploic, posterior gastric, pancreatica magna, hilar branches.
- Exam trap: right gastroepiploic is from gastroduodenal (common hepatic), left gastroepiploic is from splenic.

Reference: Last's Anatomy, 13th edition, abdomen (coeliac trunk and splenic artery); Gray's Anatomy, 41st edition, arteries of the stomach and spleen; StatPearls, Anatomy, Abdomen and Pelvis: Arteries (https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK525959); PMC review of gastric blood supply (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12651528/).

1258.explanation:
Correct answer: D — Splenic

Why this is correct:
- The arteria pancreatica magna is one of the largest pancreatic branches of the splenic artery. It usually arises from the middle or distal part of the splenic artery as it runs along the upper border of the pancreas, and it supplies the body and tail of the pancreas, anastomosing with other pancreatic vessels.
- The splenic artery itself is the largest branch of the coeliac trunk; its other branches include short gastric, posterior gastric, left gastroepiploic (left gastro-omental), smaller pancreatic branches and terminal hilar branches.
- By contrast, the left gastric artery supplies the lesser curvature and oesophageal end of the stomach; the right gastric artery is a branch of the hepatic artery proper; and the common hepatic artery gives the gastroduodenal artery (whence the right gastroepiploic arises) and hepatic arterial branches.
- Therefore arteria pancreatica magna is a splenic artery branch and the answer is D.

Clinical reasoning:
| Step | Finding | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Named vessel 'arteria pancreatica magna' | A major artery to the body/tail of the pancreas |
| 2 | Trace its parent artery backwards | It arises from the splenic artery along the pancreatic upper border |
| 3 | Contrast with gastric arteries | Left gastric, right gastric and common hepatic supply stomach/duodenum/hepatic bed instead |

Why other options are wrong:
- Option A — Left gastric artery arises directly from the coeliac trunk and runs along the lesser curvature; it gives oesophageal branches but not the pancreatica magna.
- Option B — Right gastric artery arises from the hepatic artery proper (or its left branch) and supplies the pyloric lesser curvature.
- Option C — Common hepatic artery is a coeliac trunk branch that gives gastroduodenal and hepatic arteries; the pancreatica magna is not among its branches.

Key points:
- Arteria pancreatica magna = branch of splenic artery; it is a high-yield landmark of the coeliac axis.
- Exam trap: pair it with item 1258 — right gastroepiploic comes from gastroduodenal/common hepatic, not splenic.

Reference: Last's Anatomy, 13th edition, abdomen (splenic artery and pancreas); Gray's Anatomy, 41st edition, splenic artery branches; StatPearls, Anatomy, Abdomen and Pelvis: Arteries (https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK525959); Woodburne, The Arteries of the Pancreas (https://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/bitstreams/da0e649f-bc7d-400c-864e-b5c6dc61df2d/download).
